## UniFFI — yes, still the direction, with two caveats

Per the freshly-reset ADR ledger: **legacy decision 0030 (UniFFI/C-ABI two-surface split) is "Current," explicitly "amended by ADR-0072."** And #2125 (M14: migrate lifecycle/binding/capability FFI to UniFFI) is open, with M14-0 already landed (#2149). So: [...] Assistant: Now your UniFFI question — this is the important one, and you're right to press on it.

## You're right. The burden of proof is on *keeping* two surfaces, and it hasn't been met.

"A for X, B for Y" has burned this project repeatedly — and it's documented: the half-migrated C-ABI symbols, the `dispatch_action` JSON shim, the ~30 residual dual JNI lanes, the compat-alias sweeps. Every one of those is the *same failure*: two binding paths for the same platform, so every feature has to pick a lane and things rot half-migrated. That's an SSOT violation, and your instinct against it matches doctrine better than legacy decision 0030 does. In fact **legacy decision 0030 ("two-surface split") is exactly one of the "bucket B" items the clean-break spine should re-examine** — 0069–0073's whole thesis is *fewer public doors, fewer duplicate recipes*, and a dual ABI is the opposite.
topic: The user is probing whether to adopt UniFFI as a single binding surface or keep the dual C-ABI/UniFFI split.

evidence_text:
User: I asked an agent about the status of uniffi and it recommended we revisit the current scope of adopting uniffi -- my instict tells me to go with a single solution -- please launch an xhigh agent to review and fixup the scope of our refactor to fold in the adoption of uniffi correctly -- here is what the agent found (just for reference in case some of this is useful) Now your UniFFI question — this is the important one, and you're right to press on it.

You're right. The burden of proof is on keeping two surfaces, and it hasn't been met.

"A for X, B for Y" has burned this project repeatedly — and it's documented: the half-migrated C-ABI symbols, the dispatch_action JSON shim, the ~30 residual dual JNI lanes, the compat-alias sweeps. Every one of those is the same failure: two binding paths for the same platform, so every feature has to pick a lane and things rot half-migrated. That's an SSOT violation, and your instinct against it matches doctrine better than legacy decision 0030 does. In fact legacy decision 0030 ("two-surface split") is exactly one of the "bucket B" items the clean-break spine should re-examine — 0069–0073's whole thesis is fewer public doors, fewer duplicate recipes, and a dual ABI is the opposite. [...] The browser will always be a separate binding — wasm-bindgen, because UniFFI doesn't target wasm. But that's one surface per platform family (native=UniFFI, web=wasm-bindgen), which is unavoidable and fine. It is not the "two ABIs for the same platform" trap. So "UniFFI for everything" precisely means one surface for all of native (iOS/Android/desktop).

My stance

Default to UniFFI-for-everything-native, single surface, and put the burden of proof on anyone who wants to keep a byte lane. Concretely, reframe #2125 from "migrate lifecycle/binding/capability to UniFFI" into a measured bake-off: prove whether UniFFI (carrying FlatBuffer bytes, via stream or callback) can sustain the projection push at acceptable latency.
- If yes (likely, post-0055) → collapse to UniFFI-only on native. That deletes the entire half-migration bug class — the recurring tax you're describing.
- If a measured wall remains → keep a narrow byte lane, but as an internal optimization behind the single UniFFI surface, documented with numbers — never a second public ABI you choose per-feature.

So: yes, it should be one surface, and you're right that the split is a smell. The only thing standing in front of "UniFFI for everything native" is an unverified perf assumption — and the right move is to measure it, not inherit it
topic: The user is probing the adoption scope of UniFFI and whether to unify on a single binding surface for all native platforms instead of maintaining dual C-ABI + UniFFI paths.

evidence_text:
- nip05 fetches are **user-initiated**. AD's embed-render moment is **passively triggered by rendering someone else's note** — any attacker who gets one event in front of you can make your client beacon an HTTPS GET to an attacker-chosen domain+path. Plus a **DNS-rebinding TOCTOU** hole in the existing guard (documented in `host_guard.rs`) that `ureq` 2.x can't cleanly close.

The first comment's answer: ship it opt-in / default-off, WoT-gate later. The second opinion **disagrees on framing** and lands on the sharper recommendation: **don't do passive-on-render at all in v1** — resolve only on an explicit per-link affordance (tap/hover to expand). That collapses both product moments into one "user asked to resolve this URL" path, and sidesteps the beacon, the TOCTOU, and the feed-scale fan-out entirely. [...] - **Still open, mechanism-level (independent of policy):** the DNS-rebinding TOCTOU in `host_guard.rs`. App policy reduces *who* you beacon to, but a followed-but-hostile (or benign-linking-hostile) domain can still rebind to a private/metadata address. Resolve-then-pin (which `ureq` 2.x can't cleanly do) constrains which policies are *safe* to enable — but that's a hardening task on the shared http crate, not a reason to hardcode a default. [...] One thing worth noting: the issue still wears `status:needs-adr` and `category:decision`. Your policy-seam call resolves the main blocking product decision (open-item #1). The remaining true blocker before implementation is the **DNS-rebinding TOCTOU / resolve-then-pin** question — whether passive-fetch policies are safe to ship enabled at all given `ureq` 2.x can't pin. Once that's called, the issue is unblocked for a `nmp-nip-ad` implementation PR (paired with #2928).
topic: The user is probing whether the DNS-rebinding TOCTOU in host_guard.rs blocks passive AD resolution from being safe to ship enabled.

[...] "It literally *is* a subscription that just closes immediately" is, I think, the crux — the AD query is just a raw Nostr REQ with one filter to pinned relays, read to EOSE, then CLOSE. That's the lowest-level Nostr op there is, and the kernel already opens subscriptions under the hood for every feed/interest. So the real question Fable is now chasing isn't "what new projection do we invent" but "why isn't the one-shot subscription already exposed as a primitive, and is `open_interest` + raw filter + relay-pinning already 90% of it" (there's a prior finding — #1563 — that a bare raw filter is *already* expressible through `open_interest`). [...] NEEDS CORRECTION:

evidence_text:
User: send this design question to a fable agent -- none of this options feel right and I intuit that DynamicTargetProjection is probably something that shouldn't exist (the fact that it's in nmp-content is a big tell) [...] Bonus from the framing: the sharpest available statement of "why the four options felt wrong" —
- `RefShape::Event` is single-result BY CONSTRUCTION, not omission. `RefResolver` (`crates/nmp-core/src/kernel/refs.rs`) is a keyed identity resolver: `RefNamespace::{Profile, Event}` only, key → one entity's current bytes; `RefLiveness::Live` means tailing replacement of that same entity. Its module doc excludes the other model explicitly: "No zap_total / reply-counts; those are aggregate queries over event *sets*, a different invalidation model (ADR-0070 D2 scope limit)." A ref answers "current value of this identity"; a filter is a predicate with open-ended set membership. Category error, correctly rejected.
- `open_search` is a concept door whose demand compiler is FTS-specific by charter; the reusable part underneath (per-relay pinned ReadDemands on open_read) is what AD should ride directly.
- `DynamicTargetProjection` isn't a seam at all (Q1).
- `InterestShape::RelayPinnedFilter` misreads the type twice: `InterestShape` is a struct, and it already has `relay_pin` (shape.rs:126).
topic: The user is probing whether all four proposed #2948 options for the AD delivery primitive are architecturally wrong (category errors rather than merely narrow seams).
